analysis.one_liner: Bans former members of Congress from ever lobbying Congress and tightens lobbying disclosure rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after being introduced and referred to committee, it sat there until the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the rules for the "revolving door" between Congress and the lobbying industry. Former Senators, House members, and elected congressional officers would be barred from ever lobbying Congress again; senior congressional staff would face a six-year ban instead of one. It would also block lobbyists from being hired by the members or committees they used to lobby, create a public searchable website of lobbying disclosures, force big lobbying firms to disclose which former members and top staff they employ, and raise the maximum fine for breaking lobbying rules from $200,000 to $500,000.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who would get a searchable public record of who is lobbying whom and which former officials are now on lobbying payrolls, and whose lawmakers would face a lifetime bar on cashing in their congressional access. Taxpayers also gain indirectly from a smaller market for earmarks and influence.

how_it_helps.text: Bars former Senators, House Members, and elected congressional officers from lobbying Congress for life, up from 2 years for Senators and 1 year for House Members.
Extends the post-employment lobbying ban for senior congressional staff from 1 year to 6 years.
Requires an easily searchable public website, lobbyists.gov, consolidating lobbying disclosures, plus annual public lists of former Members and senior staff working for large lobbying firms.
Bars registered lobbyists with substantial prior lobbying contacts from being hired by the Members or committees they lobbied for six years.
Raises the civil penalty cap for lobbying disclosure violations from $200,000 to $500,000 and requires filings to be sent to the U.S. Attorney for D.C. to check for underreporting.

analysis.who_pays: Former members of Congress, senior congressional staff, and the lobbying firms that hire them, who would lose the ability to convert years in public office into lucrative influence work. Firms with more than three lobbyists would bear new disclosure and reporting costs, with fines up to $500,000 for violations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ex-lawmakers, senior staff, and lobbying firms

drawbacks.text: The ban on hiring lobbyists into congressional offices can be waived by the Senate or House ethics committee for 'compelling national need,' giving each chamber a built-in escape hatch.
A lifetime lobbying ban pushes former Members' influence work into unregistered channels—advisory roles, trade associations, and 'strategic consulting'—where the disclosure rules may not reach.
Raising the civil penalty cap to $500,000 only deters if violations are actually detected and prosecuted; the bill adds referral to one U.S. Attorney but little new investigative capacity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits—slower and smaller revolving door, better public disclosure—are real but modest; wealthy former officials can wait out or work around restrictions, and enforcement depends on prosecutors. The costs are small in dollars and mainly fall on ex-Members who planned to sell their access. The honest drawback is that the Senate's own ethics committee could waive the lobbyist-hiring ban, softening the bill's core promise.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in August 2015; the committee never acted, and the bill expired when the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Michael Bennet introduced the Close the Revolving Door Act of 2015 on August 5, 2015, with Senator Al Franken as the other original cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
The committee took no further action on the bill; no hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded, and the bill died there when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Former members of Congress and senior staff who sell their connections to lobbying firms, and the lobbying industry that employs them, are better off because the bill never moved.

for.name: Sen. Al Franken
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action—no hearing, markup, or report—leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Senate leadership of the 114th Congress
against.role: Senate Majority Leader and party leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor or prioritized its consideration, so it never advanced past committee.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats, but with only two cosponsors and no votes, the bill never generated a party-line test of support.

industries.note: They would lose their most valuable product—recent Members and senior staff—and face tougher disclosure and penalties. Many firms earn a premium by advertising their insiders; a lifetime ban on Member-lobbyists and 6-year staff bans would force a business model built on congressional access to change.

industries.industry: Trade associations and corporate Washington offices
industries.note: They could no longer rent a former Member's direct line to Congress, but they could still hire ex-staff after six years and lobby through anyone who never held a congressional job. Their access advantage would shrink, not disappear.

industries.industry: Former Members of Congress and senior congressional staff
industries.note: Members would face a lifetime bar and senior staff a six-year bar on cashing in their connections through lobbying. This is the bill's central cost, and the population it targets.
